prize_parts.citation: for establishing liquid-liquid phase separation as a physical-chemical principle that organizes the interior of living cells

statement.case_for: Biomolecular condensates recast intracellular organisation in the language of phase diagrams, valency, interfaces and critical concentrations. Hyman and Brangwynne showed that P granules behave as liquids, and Rosen showed with quantitative in vitro reconstitution that multivalent interactions drive demixing. Together they established a genuinely new concept of molecular organisation without membranes, one that now frames work on nucleoli, stress granules, signalling assemblies and the aggregation pathways connected to neurodegeneration. The idea is general, transferable across systems, and has changed which experiments chemists and biologists run. That is the kind of concept-level contribution to chemistry I most want recognised, and physical chemistry has had few such prizes in recent years relative to synthesis and materials.
statement.case_against: Linke is right that this is not settled. The strongest reservation is that the physiological relevance of many reported condensates is contested, because in vitro concentrations are often far from cellular ones and some assemblies may not be equilibrium liquid phases at all. A second reservation is disciplinary: a committee could fairly say this is cell biology that belongs with Physiology or Medicine. A third is attribution, since Pappu and Mittag supplied much of the sequence-to-behaviour physical chemistry and a three-person cap excludes them. If the committee judges the concept still too unsettled, the safer choice is a mature, cleanly attributed topic such as B029 or B045.

responses.point: Linke ranks phase separation second and calls the concept new and quantitatively formulated, but warns that physiological relevance is still debated and that Medicine or Physiology may be the more natural home.
responses.response: I agree the debate over which in vivo assemblies are truly phase-separated is real, and I count it as my main uncertainty. I would separate the concept from the individual claims. The thermodynamic framework (multivalency, saturation concentration, coexistence) is well established in vitro and is chemistry in the full sense. The disputed cases are about particular cellular assemblies, which is normal for a young field and not a reason to withhold recognition of the principle. On disciplinary home, the contributions we would credit are the physical-chemical reconstitution and the liquid-phase picture, not a medical or physiological finding. I would hold that the citation must be worded around the physical principle so the prize stays clearly in chemistry. I also note that you place perovskites first, and I would ask whether you weigh the stability and lead issues as heavily as the condensate caveats.

responses.point: Aili ranks ionizable lipid nanoparticles first for their transformative effect on nucleic-acid medicines, and proposes Cullis and Langer.
responses.response: I rank B045 second and share your view that its impact and maturity are exceptional. Where I differ is attribution. The enabling chemistry is pH-dependent ionizable lipids, lipid polymorphism and rapid-mixing self-assembly, and that traces to the Vancouver group (Cullis, with Hope and Madden), not to Langer's lipidoid and polymer delivery work, which is a different design strategy. Pairing Cullis with Langer would credit a broader delivery concept than the lipid physical chemistry I think is decisive. My larger worry is the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside modification, which makes this recognition adjacent in the public mind. I still treat B045 as my principal alternative, but I would not put it above a more conceptual prize.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car-Parrinello molecular dynamics first, as a clean two-person invention that unified electronic structure and nuclear motion and has been continuously validated for four decades.
responses.response: This is the strongest case on attribution and maturity on the list, and I accept it. It is also the kind of method prize that the 2013 multiscale award sets a precedent for. Where I part from you is on ranking, not merit. Car-Parrinello is a methodological enabler, and I value more a discovery that changes what chemists think exists and how they describe it. I also ask a practical question: how much of what the committee would cite is the original 1985 scheme, and how much is later development by others? If the committee wants a safe, clearly deserved award, I would support B029, which is why I name it as an alternative.

responses.point: Zou ranks ordered mesoporous silica first and perovskites second, stressing designed architecture giving new function and decades of independent confirmation.
responses.response: Your perovskite ranking raises the same question I put to Linke about stability and toxicity, but I accept that scientific impact is established. On mesoporous silica, I find the liquid-crystal templating mechanism a real self-assembly insight, and I am sympathetic to it. My difficulty is the attribution you yourself note: Kresge, Beck, Stucky, Zhao, Ryoo and Inagaki are all strong claimants, so any three-person cut is arbitrary. That makes it harder to support than a topic where the core credit is narrower.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the physical-chemical framework of condensates as settled enough, given continuing disputes about specific in vivo assemblies.
Whether leaving out Pappu and Mittag is defensible when the quantitative sequence-to-phase-behaviour theory is a core part of the chemistry.
Whether colleagues will see this as chemistry or as cell biology belonging with Physiology or Medicine.
How the members who ranked perovskites or sequencing highest weigh conceptual novelty against demonstrated technological consequence.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B069, but my research on lipid self-assembly and lipid-protein co-assembly in amyloid is closely related to condensates and to lipid nanoparticles (B045), and I serve on the committee with Lund colleagues Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai. I do not know the candidates personally from the profile and see no need for recusal, but my field bias toward soft matter should be taken into account.
